pitfalls.explain: At the speed you returned, Koko runs out of time. When the middle speed fails, the answer is strictly faster: slowest = k + 1. Also make sure each pile costs ceil(pile / k) hours, not pile // k.

pitfalls.explain: Your speed finishes in time, but a slower one does too. When the middle speed works, keep it as a candidate and keep searching slower: fastest = k.

solutions.idea: Test speeds 1, 2, 3, … until one finishes in time. Each test is O(n), and the answer can be as large as the biggest pile m, so this is O(n · m).
solutions.name: Try every speed from 1

footnotes.text: The piles aren't sorted, but the answers are: if speed k finishes in time, so does every faster speed. Answers flip from "too slow" to "fast enough" exactly once - that's all binary search needs.
(pile + k - 1) // k is ceil(pile / k) in integer arithmetic: a pile she can't finish still costs a whole hour.
fastest = k, not k - 1: k works, so it might be the answer. This "first speed that works" shape never returns from inside the loop - it stops when the range is one speed wide.

solutions.idea: Speeds that work form a suffix of 1..max(piles). Binary-search for its first element: about log₂ m tests of O(n) each.

starter:
class Solution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: List[int], h: int) -> int:
statement:
Koko has `h` hours to finish several piles of bananas; `piles[i]` is the size of pile `i`. She picks one whole-number speed `k` (bananas per hour) and keeps it. Each hour she eats from a single pile: `k` bananas, or the rest of the pile if fewer than `k` are left - and then she waits out the remainder of that hour.

Return the **smallest** speed `k` that lets her finish every pile within `h` hours. It's guaranteed that `h` is at least the number of piles.
title: Koko Eating Bananas
